clue.text: Medal, eg when polished, gave off reflected light

indicators.note: polishing reworks the surface, so the letters of the medal and eg are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A medal, once buffed up, catches the light and shines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when polished' looks like part of the picture of shining metal, but it is the anagram signal working on MEDAL and EG together.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that shone with reflected brightness can be said to have glinted or sparkled, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Good money, they say, for one following the stars

indicators.note: they say signals that the money word is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: the rupee is the currency of India and Pakistan

explanation.surface: Good money is said to go to anyone who follows celebrities.
explanation.walkthrough: RUPEE spoken sounds like ROUPIE, which follows G.
explanation.definitionFit: A groupie is a devoted fan who follows pop stars or celebrities around on tour.

clue.text: Town Eve and Henry go around occasionally

indicators.note: going round suggests the letters circulate into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Two people called Eve and Henry go round the town from time to time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go around' is the anagram signal on all fifteen letters of TOWN EVE AND HENRY.
explanation.definitionFit: Happening at irregular intervals, from time to time, is the meaning of this adverbial phrase.

clue.text: Runner in a pickle over the rough green

parts.note: a pickle is a mess, a difficult situation

indicators.note: rough here means roughed up, so the letters of green are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A golfer in trouble runs over the rough towards the green.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' puts MESS above ENGER (from 'rough' on GREEN) in this down entry. 'Rough' and 'green' look like golf, but rough is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A messenger runs errands carrying messages, so a runner in the old sense of courier.

clue.text: End of old part of shoe that's remained

indicators.note: the end of a word means its final letter

parts.note: the welt is the strip of leather joining a shoe's upper to its sole

explanation.surface: The worn end of an old shoe part is the only bit that has survived.
explanation.definitionFit: Dwelt is the past tense of dwell, meaning stayed or lived in a place.

clue.text: Worrying when joining outside society

indicators.note: the word for joining sits outside, wrapping round the letter for society

parts.note: fusing is joining things together

explanation.surface: Someone frets at the prospect of joining some outside club or society.
explanation.definitionFit: Fretting and fussing are both forms of anxious, agitated behaviour, so the words are synonyms here.

clue.text: Dish from the Continent doesn't get a n-notice

indicators.note: the continent goes without the a that follows, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: Africa is one of the continents
notice means see, and the stammered 'n-' asks for the word with its first letter doubled in a stutter

explanation.surface: A dish from mainland Europe gets no attention from a stammering diner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Continent' looks like mainland Europe and French cooking, but it is AFRICA, which loses A to give FRICA. The stutter in 'n-notice' says SEE is stuttered too, as S-SEE.
explanation.definitionFit: A fricassee is a dish of stewed or fried meat pieces served in a thick white sauce.

clue.text: The Adriatic resort for a break

definitions.meaning: the port and holiday city on the Croatian Dalmatian coast
a crack or division where something has come apart

explanation.definitionFit: The Croatian coastal city shares its name with the noun for a crack or rupture.

clue.text: Weakly, at first, I left for mostly material possessions

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Weakly, at first, I left for mostly material possessions' (15) for INSUBSTANTIALLY: 'Weakly' defines, but no parse found turns the rest into IN-SUBSTANTIALLY; a search found no blog to confirm the setter's wordplay.
annotationWithheld.clue: Weakly, at first, I left for mostly material possessions

clue.text: Wanders about without secure contrivances

indicators.note: without in the old sense of outside, so the wandering word wraps the securing word

parts.note: to gad about is to wander around in search of pleasure
to get is to secure or obtain

explanation.surface: Someone drifts around without any secure tricks up their sleeve.
explanation.definitionFit: Gadgets are small mechanical devices or ingenious contraptions, so contrivances is a synonym.

clue.text: Umpire's call, distinctive, upset side too much in one aspect

parts.note: in cricket the umpire calls 'over' at the end of six balls
special means distinctive or out of the ordinary

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters of side are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cricket umpire's distinctive call upsets one team, who think he is too narrow in his focus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Umpire's call' points to cricket, where the umpire ends each set of six balls with this word; 'upset' is the anagram signal on the word side.
explanation.definitionFit: Being specialised beyond reason means concentrating excessively on a single narrow area or field.

clue.text: One getting the cash? Yes, in certain exercises

indicators.note: the word for yes is placed in the letters for the exercises

parts.note: PE is physical education, the school exercise lesson
aye is an old or dialect word for yes, also used when voting

explanation.surface: Someone asks who gets paid, and the answer comes back yes, for certain exercise classes.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who receives a payment is the one to whom the money is paid out.

clue.text: Large area with power is easy to control

parts.note: a tract is a large expanse of land
able means having the power or capability to do something

explanation.surface: A large estate that comes with power is said to be easy to manage.
explanation.definitionFit: A tractable person or animal is docile and manageable, readily handled or directed by others.

clue.text: Gone stale possibly, so pulls out

indicators.note: possibly suggests these letters could be arranged another way

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Bread that has gone stale is perhaps pulled apart and thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' signals the anagram of GONE STALE; 'so' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To lengthen something by stretching is to draw or pull it out, the sense of extending.

clue.text: Trials about public transport in the lab

indicators.note: the word for trials goes round the word for public transport

parts.note: tests are trials
the Tube is London's underground railway

explanation.surface: Experiments on public transport are carried out under laboratory conditions.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: these glass tubes are things found in the lab. The Tube is London's underground railway.
explanation.definitionFit: Test tubes are the narrow glass vessels used for experiments, standard equipment in a laboratory.

clue.text: Hymnist's measure of power

definitions.meaning: Isaac ... was the English hymn writer of 'O God, Our Help in Ages Past'; the 's stands for 'is'
the watt is the SI unit of power, so several of them measure it

explanation.definitionFit: The surname of the hymn writer Isaac Watts coincides with the plural of the electrical unit of power.

clue.text: Server missing one with pool, playing game

indicators.note: missing means lacking, so the letter for one is dropped

parts.note: a waiter serves at table
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters of pool are played around with

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A waiter who is missing has gone off to the pool to play a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missing' drops I from WAITER to give WATER; 'playing' turns POOL into POLO.
explanation.definitionFit: Water polo is a team ball game played in a swimming pool.

clue.text: Learner recorded within "reasonable ability"

indicators.note: the letter for learner is set down inside the word for reasonable

parts.note: fair means reasonable or moderately good
L is the learner, as on British L-plates

explanation.surface: A driving learner's ability is written down in quotes as merely reasonable.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition and the word 'reasonable' overlap: 'reasonable ability' defines, while 'reasonable' alone supplies FAIR. L is the learner, from the L-plates British learner drivers display.
explanation.definitionFit: Flair is a natural talent or aptitude, a knack that marks out real ability.

clue.text: Driftwood? Fellow collects plenty before noon

parts.note: lots means plenty
AM, ante meridiem, means before noon

explanation.surface: A man gathers loads of driftwood on the beach before midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collects' is a link joining F to the rest. The question mark admits the definition is an example: driftwood is one kind of floating wreckage.
explanation.definitionFit: Flotsam is wreckage or debris found floating on the sea, of which driftwood is an example.

clue.text: An inducement for the char, possibly

definitions.meaning: a bribe or extra offered to persuade someone
char is British slang for tea, and sugar or a sugar substitute is added to it

explanation.definitionFit: A sweetener is both a bribe-like incentive and something such as sugar stirred into tea to sweeten it.

clue.text: Concerns for best wishes

definitions.meaning: the verb sense, as in 'this concerns you', meaning relates to
the sign-off in a letter, as in 'kind ...'

explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb meaning relates to or has to do with and a noun for friendly greetings.

clue.text: Art models represented in classical painting

indicators.note: represented means presented again, so the letters of art models are set out anew

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Life models in an art class are depicted in an old classical painting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'represented' is the anagram signal on ART MODELS.
explanation.definitionFit: A painting by a great European artist from before about 1800 is called by this name.

clue.text: A book on the Mob making a WMD

indicators.note: making means making something new out of, so the letters of mob are reworked

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A book on organised crime describes the gangsters building a weapon of mass destruction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' puts B above OMB in this down entry; 'making' turns MOB into OMB.
explanation.definitionFit: An atomic bomb is the classic example of a weapon of mass destruction, abbreviated WMD.

clue.text: It's what Barry and Gary do

definitions.text: It's what Barry and Gary do

parts.words: It's what Barry and Gary do
parts.note: the two names share their ending sound, so the clue is a description of what they do with each other, not of any action by two men

explanation.definitionFit: Two words that end in the same sound are said to chime, as Barry and Gary do.

clue.text: Being in charge, left off feeling remorse

indicators.note: off means removed, so the letter for left is dropped from the word for being in charge

parts.note: ruling means being in charge or governing

explanation.surface: A leader, ousted from power, regrets what happened.
explanation.definitionFit: To rue something is to regret it, so the present participle means feeling sorry or regretful.

clue.text: Slip out of form?

parts.note: a 'form' is a school class in Britain, so a slip from one is a pupil's comic blunder, while 'out of form' suggests a dip in performance

explanation.definitionFit: A howler is a glaring mistake, and a pupil's comic error in an exam is the classic example.

clue.text: Small business, in short, could be on the way

parts.note: mini means small

indicators.note: in short means cut down, so the word business is abbreviated to its opening letters

parts.note: the word business, shortened

explanation.surface: A small business, to put it briefly, might soon be up and running.
explanation.definitionFit: A small bus for a handful of passengers is a vehicle one may meet on the road.

clue.text: Kim is one of those having cash in the monetary system

indicators.note: the cash is placed inside the letters for the monetary system

parts.note: EMS is the European Monetary System
a pony is British slang for twenty-five pounds

explanation.surface: Someone named Kim is one of a group of people with money tied up in the European currency system.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having' is a link. Kim is Kipling's novel, named after its hero, so the hero is an example of the answer; a pony is £25 in British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's novel takes its title from its hero Kim, so his name is an example of a person giving a name to something.
